questions.prompt: What pressure makes Operation Crush a revealing OKR case in this chapter?
choices: Intel faced a real competitive threat that made internal drift costly
Intel was enjoying stable growth and revisiting long-term culture
The company had too little technical talent to compete at all

explanation.gentle: The chapter begins with a real threat, so scattered priorities and slow feedback become dangerous quickly.
explanation.direct: The case matters because pressure exposed whether the company could align fast enough to matter.
explanation.competitive: The story is not about a calm planning season. It is about drift becoming expensive under threat.

questions.prompt: Why did one objective matter so much in Operation Crush?
choices: It let each department define urgency in its own way
It gave the company one shared line of sight for coordinated execution
It removed the need for feedback from the field

explanation.gentle: One visible priority helped different functions work toward the same fight instead of protecting separate agendas.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats one objective as the mechanism that turned urgency into direction across the company.
explanation.competitive: One fight beats six private emergencies. That is the point.

questions.prompt: What role did field feedback play in the chapter logic?
choices: It was optional once management had chosen the priority
It made the story more democratic but did not affect execution
It kept company-wide focus connected to reality while the fight was live

explanation.gentle: Field truth mattered because leaders needed reality quickly enough to adjust.
explanation.direct: Upward feedback is part of the operating loop here, not a soft extra.
explanation.competitive: A blind command chain is just panic with titles.

questions.prompt: Aria team treats six different issues as simultaneous emergencies after a competitor move. What response best fits the chapter?
choices: Preserve all six so no team feels ignored
Choose one priority that outranks the rest and align the week around it
Delay any decision until every group fully agrees

explanation.gentle: The chapter would narrow the fight so effort can reinforce itself.
explanation.direct: Operation Crush logic says to define urgency through one visible objective, not let every alarm survive.
explanation.competitive: If every emergency lives, none of them leads.

questions.prompt: Janelle competition team stayed late, worked hard, and still entered the round with conflicting priorities. What failure does this show?
choices: Urgency without coordinated alignment
Too much upward feedback from the field
A lack of any meaningful deadline pressure

explanation.gentle: The room had intensity but not one shared fight.
explanation.direct: This is the chapter distinction between looking urgent and actually coordinating execution.
explanation.competitive: Sweat is not a substitute for alignment.

questions.prompt: Why is it a weak reading to say Operation Crush proves panic creates excellence?
choices: Because the chapter says fear itself sharpened the organization
Because the chapter says the mechanism was disciplined focus plus fast truth flow, not emergency emotion
Because the chapter avoids discussing pressure altogether

explanation.gentle: The useful lesson is disciplined concentration, not permanent emergency feeling.
explanation.direct: The chapter warns against confusing adrenaline with the mechanism that produced execution.
explanation.competitive: If panic were the engine, every frantic company would become excellent.

questions.prompt: Hugo leadership team trusts a clean dashboard while field technicians are reporting a new defect pattern. According to the chapter, what is the main risk?
choices: The company is aligned too strongly around one objective
The response becomes brittle because leadership is acting on stale reality
The field team should stop surfacing problems until the weekly review

explanation.gentle: Company-wide focus still needs reality to travel upward quickly.
explanation.direct: Alignment hardens into error when leaders stop hearing live signals from the field.
explanation.competitive: A neat dashboard can become a disciplined way to stay wrong.

questions.prompt: A robotics lab keeps four late-stage ambitions alive before inspection day. Which judgment fits the chapter best?
choices: Parallel ambition is safer because it honors every subgroup
The team should choose the one rescue goal that most changes the outcome
The team should avoid deciding until the last night reveals the answer

explanation.gentle: The chapter favors deliberate narrowing when time pressure makes spread attention costly.
explanation.direct: One rescue goal creates coordinated action; parallel ambition preserves drift.
explanation.competitive: Calling refusal to choose teamwork is the trap.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter hardest tension about crisis leadership?
choices: Crisis should become the permanent model because it keeps people sharp
Crisis can reveal disciplined execution while also tempting leaders to depend on emergency intensity
Crisis matters only because it increases top-down control

explanation.gentle: The case clarifies priorities, but the chapter warns against treating alarm itself as the source of excellence.
explanation.direct: The tension is between learning from crisis clarity and becoming addicted to crisis as a management style.
explanation.competitive: Use the clarity. Do not start worshipping the siren.

questions.prompt: Why does Chapter 3 naturally point toward a chapter about choosing priorities before crisis?
choices: Because the book now wants to abandon execution stories for biography
Because the case suggests strong leaders should build clear priority discipline before emergency removes all slack
Because Operation Crush worked only because Intel stayed in constant crisis mode

explanation.gentle: The bridge asks what disciplined leaders should do before pressure makes the choice for them.
explanation.direct: If one-priority focus is powerful in crisis, the next question is how to choose deliberately before the clock compresses everything.
explanation.competitive: Real leaders do not wait for the fire alarm to tell them what matters.
